questions.explanation: Reading backwards from the last index with an inclusive lower bound of zero visits every element, and the invariant that i is the count of elements still unread is exactly what lets the test be written as i >= 0. The loop adds 9, then 5, then 2, giving 16. Reading 14 believes the update runs before the test, which would drop the 2; reading 9 believes the loop stops after the first element; reading 7 believes the small element is the one left out.

questions.explanation: The three valid indices of a three-element array are 0, 1 and 2, so a header is correct exactly when its counter takes those three values and no others. A strict bound against a.length runs 0, 1 and 2 and then fails on 3. Bounding the counter by a.length - 1 with an inclusive test produces the same three values, because 2 is the last one that satisfies it. Bounding against a.length itself adds the value 3, which is not an index at all, and starting the counter at 1 omits index 0 while still stopping correctly at the end.
questions.hint: Write the counter values for each header and compare them with 0, 1 and 2.
questions.learningObjective: judge which index-loop headers cover exactly the valid indices of an array
